title: Stock Market Simulator
subtitle: Twelve weeks. Ten thousand rupees. Six made-up companies. Buy, sell or hold, and see what the news does.
open.hint: Twelve weeks of news, prices and your own choices.
co.chaiwala.name: Chaiwala Ltd
co.deccan_farms.name: Deccan Farms
co.hyd_repairs.name: Hyd Mobile Repairs
co.charminar_textiles.name: Charminar Textiles
co.musi_transport.name: Musi Transport
co.bhagya_tech.name: Bhagya Tech
news.n1: Markets are open. You have {cash} and six companies to choose from. Each week you can buy, sell or hold.
news.n2: Chaiwala Ltd opens 20 new tea stalls. Its owners expect more sales.
news.n3: A famous cricketer is seen drinking chai on TV. Nothing about any company's business has changed.
news.n4: Chat feed: "Everyone is buying Deccan Farms! Get in now before it jumps more!" No company news came with it.
news.n5: Deccan Farms says the rumour was untrue. Its rains came late and its harvest will be small.
news.n6: Dividend week. Companies share part of their profit with owners, paid on each share you hold.
news.n7: Musi Transport wins a city bus contract. It expects steady income for years.
news.n8: Worrying news about the economy. Prices fall across the whole market.
news.n9: Hyd Mobile Repairs opens a new shop. Charminar Textiles has a slow festival season.
news.n10: Bhagya Tech loses its biggest customer and shuts down. Its shares are now almost worthless.
news.n11: A calm week. Some prices recover a little.
news.n12: Final week. Dividends are paid again, and then the market closes.
intro.title: How it works
intro.1: Each week a headline arrives and prices move.
intro.2: You buy and sell whole shares. Every trade costs {fee} of its value.
intro.3: In two of the weeks, companies pay dividends to their owners.
intro.4: Not every headline matters, and not every price move has a reason.
intro.5: Your money is shown beside the market. After every move, a coach tells you what it did.
news.label: This week
err.cash: Not enough cash for that, including the fee.
err.holding: You do not hold that many shares.
done.sell: Sold {qty} of {name} and received {total}, after a fee of {fee}.
end.last: End the game and see how it went
dividend.paid: Dividends of {amount} were paid into your cash.
debrief.title: How it went
debrief.result: You ended with {value}. That is {gain} ({pct}) from the {cash} you started with.
debrief.trades: You made {n} trades. Fees took {fees} of your money.
debrief.noTrades: You made no trades, so you paid no fees.
moves.title: What moved each price
moves.nothing: No headline moved it much. It drifted with the market.
moves.failed: It shut down, and its shares fell to almost nothing.
spread.title: How spread out you were
spread.none: You held only cash at the end, so no company could help or hurt you.
spread.one: You held just one company at the end. If it falls or fails, your whole amount takes the hit.
spread.concentrated: You held {count} companies, but {top} of your shares sat in one. A fall there would hurt most.
spread.some: You held {count} companies. Your money was partly spread out.
spread.spread: You held {count} companies, with no single one above {top} of your shares. A fall in one would hurt less.
moments.title: Three moments to look at
moments.rumour.yes: In week {round}, a chat rumour pushed {name} up with no real news. You bought {qty} shares that week. A week later the price fell back. Many people buy because everyone else is buying.
moments.rumour.no: In week {round}, a chat rumour pushed {name} up with no real news. You did not buy it that week.
moments.drop.yes: In week {round}, the whole market fell. You sold shares that week. Selling after a fall turns a paper loss into a real one.
moments.drop.no: In week {round}, the whole market fell. You did not sell that week.
moments.fail.yes: {name} shut down while you held it. A single company can fail, and its shares can go to almost zero.
moments.fail.no: {name} shut down. You did not hold it that week.
compare.title: The same market, a quiet approach
compare.body: If you had split your {cash} evenly over all six companies in week 1 and simply held, you would have ended with {value}, which is {gain}. You ended with {yours}.
compare.note: This is one market. A quiet approach is not always better, and none of this is advice.
next.title: What might the next 12 weeks hold for what you own?
next.note: Simulation based on made-up numbers. Dividends and news are left out.
check.title: Check what you learned
money.title: Your money
money.none: You hold no shares yet. Your money is all cash.
money.paperNote: A paper gain or loss is only locked in when you sell.
coach.title: What your move did
coach.empty: Buy, sell or end the week, and I will tell you what it did to your money.
coach.trade.buy: You bought {qty} of {name} at {price} each and paid {total}, including a {fee} fee. Your total value dipped by the fee right away.
coach.trade.sell: You sold {qty} of {name} at {price} each and received {total}, after a {fee} fee.
coach.sell.gain: You paid an average of {avg} for those shares, so this sale locks in a gain of {amount} after fees.
coach.sell.loss: You paid an average of {avg} for those shares, so this sale locks in a loss of {amount} after fees.
coach.sell.even: You sold for about what you paid, so the fee is the only cost.
coach.sell.failed: {name} has shut down, so these shares are nearly worthless. Selling at least frees the little that is left.
coach.think.breakeven: After this buying fee, and a selling fee later, {name} must rise about {pct} before you are even.
coach.think.rumour: This jump started with a chat rumour, not company news. Who gains if you rush in? Did anything real change?
coach.think.jump: {name} rose {pct} this week. Prices that jump can fall back. What real news is behind it?
coach.think.dip: {name} fell {pct} this week. A lower price is not the same as good value. Why did it fall?
coach.think.concentrated: {pct} of your shares are in {name}. If one company fails, that part takes the whole hit.
coach.spread.ok: Your shares are spread over {count} companies. A fall in one would hurt less.
coach.think.lowCash: You have little cash left. To act on new news, you would have to sell something first.
coach.think.fees: Fees so far: {fees}, which is {pct} of your starting money. Frequent trading costs add up.
coach.think.soldDrop: You sold while the whole market was falling. Selling turns a paper loss into a real one. Nobody knows if prices will recover.
coach.think.allCash: You now hold only cash. No company can hurt you, but none can help you either.
coach.week.moved: Week {n}: your total value went from {from} to {to}, a change of {delta}.
coach.week.driver: {name} made the biggest difference, {delta}, because its price moved {pct}.
coach.week.cashOnly: You held only cash, so this week's price moves did not touch your money.
coach.week.heldDrop: You held through a market-wide fall. This is a paper loss for now. It becomes real only if you sell, and nobody can promise a recovery.
coach.week.failedHeld: {name} shut down while you held {qty} shares. They lost {loss} of value. This is the risk of a single company.
coach.week.failedNot: {name} shut down. You did not hold it, so your money was not hit.
coach.week.dividend: Dividends of {amount} arrived, only for the shares you held.
coach.week.noise: That headline changed nothing about any business, yet prices still moved. Prices wobble from week to week for many reasons.
assume.fee: Each trade costs {fee} of its value.
assume.prices: Prices move by a small steady drift, random weekly swings, and the news.
check.c1.prompt: Asha buys {shares} shares at {price} each with a {feeRate} fee. The price rises to {nowPrice} and she receives {divPS} per share in dividends. What is her profit? Type a number in rupees.
check.c1.hint: Price gain, plus dividends, minus the fee.
check.c1.explain: The price gain, plus the dividends, minus the {fee} fee, leaves {profit}.
check.c2.prompt: She buys {bigSpend} of shares with a {feeRate} fee. How much is the fee? Type a number in rupees.
check.c2.hint: The fee rate times the amount.
check.c3.prompt: What does owning a share mean?
check.c3.opt.a: You own a small part of the company
check.c3.opt.b: You have lent money to the company
check.c3.opt.d: You now work for the company
check.c3.fb.c: A share guarantees nothing. Its price can fall, and the company can fail.
check.c3.hint: Think about a tea stall cut into equal parts.
check.c3.explain: A share is a small piece of ownership. It guarantees nothing.
check.c4.prompt: A chat says everyone is buying a company, and it jumped 14% this week with no company news. What is a good first question?
check.c4.opt.a: Is there real news about the business behind this jump?
check.c4.opt.b: How fast can I buy before it rises more?
check.c4.opt.c: Which friend sent me this message?
check.c4.opt.d: How many shares can I afford?
check.c4.fb.b: Rushing in because others are buying is chasing hype. A price can fall back as fast as it rose.
check.c4.hint: Think about what happened to Deccan Farms the week after the rumour.
check.c4.explain: A jump without real news can reverse. Ask what is behind it before you buy.
check.c5.prompt: Asha puts all her money in one company, and it shuts down. What is left?
check.c5.opt.a: Almost nothing, because one failure hits all of it
check.c5.opt.b: Her money is safe, because one good company is enough
check.c5.fb.b: A single company can fail. With everything in it, the whole amount takes the hit.
check.c5.hint: Remember what happened to Bhagya Tech.
check.c5.explain: With all the money in one company, one failure takes almost all of it.
